question: The speed of sound in air is about 343 m/s at room temperature. What happens to its speed when it travels through water?
solution:
The correct answer is __**It increases**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Sound is a **mechanical longitudinal wave** that requires a **material medium** (solid, liquid, or gas) for its propagation. It cannot travel through a **vacuum**.
 
• The speed of sound depends on the **density** and **elasticity** (specifically the **Bulk Modulus** in fluids) of the medium through which it travels.
 
• In **air** at **20°C** (room temperature), the speed of sound is approximately **343 m/s**. When sound moves from air into **water**, its speed increases significantly to approximately **1480 m/s** to **1500 m/s**. ***Hence, the statement that the speed increases is correct.***
 
• The primary reason for this increase is that **water** is much less **compressible** than **air**. While water is denser than air, its **elastic properties** (resistance to compression) are so much greater that the wave energy is transferred much more rapidly between molecules.
 
• Sound waves travel fastest in **solids**, followed by **liquids**, and slowest in **gases**. For example, in **steel**, sound can travel at speeds exceeding **5000 m/s**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors Affecting Speed in Fluids:** The speed of sound in a fluid is given by the formula **v = √(B/ρ)**, where **B** is the **Bulk Modulus** and **ρ** (rho) is the **density**. Since the Bulk Modulus of **water** is much higher than that of **air**, the numerator dominates, leading to a higher velocity.
 
• **Temperature Sensitivity:** In **air**, the speed of sound increases by about **0.6 m/s** for every **1 degree Celsius** increase in **temperature**. In **seawater**, factors like **salinity** and **pressure** (depth) also play a critical role in determining the exact speed.
 
• **Applications of Sound in Water:** Because sound travels so efficiently and quickly in **water**, it is used in **SONAR** (Sound Navigation and Ranging) technology to map the ocean floor and detect underwater objects like **submarines** or **shipwrecks**.
 
• **Biological Use:** Marine mammals such as **whales** and **dolphins** rely on the high speed of sound in **water** for **echolocation** and long-distance **communication**, which can span hundreds of kilometers across the **ocean**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Frequency and Wavelength:** When sound transitions from **air** to **water**, its **frequency** remains constant (as frequency depends on the source). However, because the **speed** increases, the **wavelength** must also increase to satisfy the equation **v = fλ** (velocity = frequency × wavelength).
 
• **Acoustic Impedance:** The **density** and **speed** difference between **air** and **water** creates a high **acoustic impedance** mismatch. This is why most sound originating in the air is **reflected** off the surface of the water rather than entering it.
 
• **Comparison Data:**
 
 
• Speed in **Air** (0°C): **331 m/s**
 
• Speed in **Distilled Water** (25°C): **1497 m/s**
 
• Speed in **Sea Water**: **1531 m/s**
 
• Speed in **Iron/Steel**: **5960 m/s**
 
 
 
• **History:** The first accurate measurement of the speed of sound in **water** was conducted in **1826** by **Jean-Daniel Colladon** and **Charles-François Sturm** on **Lake Geneva**, **Switzerland**.
